title: Stage 5 — System Structure
goal: Make the app maintainable: validate input, organize the API into layers, and tame frontend state.
summary: Turn a working slice into a maintainable system — input validation, layered API, real frontend state, all via a refactor branch.

checkpoint.prompt: A POST arrives with an empty name field. What should the API return?

choices.text: 400 Bad Request, with a message saying name is required
500 Internal Server Error
201 Created, and store the empty name

checkpoint.explanation: Invalid client input is a 4xx problem — 400 Bad Request. A 500 implies the server is broken; 201 would store garbage.

checkpoint.prompt: In a layered API, where should business rules (like "duration must be positive") live?

choices.text: In a service layer, separate from route handlers and the database code
Inside the SQL query strings
In the frontend only

checkpoint.explanation: Routes handle HTTP, the data layer handles storage, and the service layer holds business logic — each with one job.

checkpoint.prompt: A route handler parses HTTP, runs raw SQL, AND formats business rules all in one function. What's the problem?

choices.text: It mixes responsibilities, so it's hard to test, reuse, and change
Nothing — fewer files is always better
It will run too slowly

checkpoint.explanation: Mixing concerns makes code rigid and untestable. Splitting into layers lets each part change independently.

checkpoint.prompt: A page that fetches a list from an API should be able to render which states?

choices.text: Loading, error, empty, and the populated list
Only the populated list
Only a spinner

checkpoint.explanation: Real data has four faces: loading, error, empty, and success. Handling all four is what makes a UI feel solid.

checkpoint.prompt: Which statement best describes a refactor?

choices.text: Changing the internal structure of code without changing its external behavior
Adding a brand-new feature
Deleting the project and starting over

checkpoint.explanation: A refactor improves structure while behavior stays the same — which is why small commits and tests make it safe.

checklist.label: API validates input and returns 400 on bad data
API split into routes, service, and data layers
Frontend handles loading, error, and empty states
Refactor done on a feature branch and merged via PR
App still works end to end after the refactor

questions.prompt: Why must the server validate input even if the frontend already does?

choices.text: Anyone can call the API directly, bypassing the frontend
Frontend validation is impossible
Servers can't be trusted

questions.explanation: Frontend validation is for UX. The server is the real boundary — anyone can send requests with curl or a script.

choices.text: Each module has one clear responsibility
Keeping all code in a single file
Separating frontend developers from backend developers

questions.explanation: Separation of concerns means each piece does one job, so changes stay local and code is easier to understand and test.

questions.prompt: Which status code signals the client sent invalid data?

choices.text: 400 Bad Request
200 OK
503 Service Unavailable

questions.explanation: 400 means the request itself was bad. The server isn't broken (5xx) and it certainly didn't succeed (2xx).

questions.prompt: What does a service layer typically hold?

choices.text: Business logic, sitting between HTTP routes and data access
CSS and styling rules
The database connection password

questions.explanation: The service layer is where business rules live, independent of how requests arrive or how data is stored.

questions.prompt: Why do refactors on a feature branch?

choices.text: To keep risky restructuring isolated and reviewable before it hits shared code
Because main doesn't allow commits
It makes the code run faster

questions.explanation: A branch isolates the change so you can review it, and revert cleanly if the refactor goes sideways.
